title: Building and Evaluating AI Agents
tagline: Build a support agent, make it measurable, find its failures, gate it with tests, red-team it, and improve accuracy and cost.
description: You will build a support agent for a tiny fictional plant shop, record everything it does, find where it fails, turn those failures into tests, red-team it, and then make it both more accurate and cheaper. Every idea comes with a small example, and Eve, the built-in tutor, is one highlight away.
audience: Beginner engineers and product managers. You can read simple code and have used a chat assistant. No machine-learning or statistics background is assumed.

verbs.name: Analyze
verbs.question: What is the agent actually doing, and where does it fail?

verbs.name: Measure
verbs.question: How often does each failure happen, and can we detect it automatically?

verbs.name: Improve
verbs.question: Which change fixes it at the lowest cost, and did it really help?

modules.title: Start Here
modules.blurb: A gentle primer for beginners: what language models, agents, tools, and traces are, and why normal testing is not enough.

modules.title: Building Agents
modules.blurb: Write the spec, build a support agent with permissions enforced in code, instrument it so its behavior is measurable, and generate the scenarios every later module uses.

modules.title: Error Analysis
modules.blurb: Turn traces into a human-owned failure taxonomy, then build validated evaluators and a prevalence estimate you can defend.

modules.title: CI/CD
modules.blurb: Turn failures into a regression suite that gates deployments, and monitor production with the same evaluators.

modules.title: Security, Safety, and Governance
modules.blurb: Map the attack surface, red-team the running agent, add guards and human approval, and keep a governance record.

modules.title: Improving Agents
modules.blurb: Compare configurations on accuracy and cost, route each fix to the cheapest layer, and run the upgrade drill when new models ship.

modules.title: Bonus
modules.blurb: Common traps in eval-focused interviews and how to avoid them.

runningExample.title: Pip's Plant Shop
runningExample.summary: A small online store that sells houseplants. Sprout is its support agent. Customers ask about orders, shipping, refunds, and plant care. Every lesson uses the same shop, the same people, and the same six tools, so you never have to re-learn the setting.

tools.name: lookup_order
tools.does: Status, items, and dates for one order

tutorNotes: Prefer the course's running example: Pip's Plant Shop, a small online plant store, and Sprout, its support agent with the tools lookup_order, get_shipping_status, search_care_guide, cancel_order (T1), issue_refund (T2, needs human approval), and escalate_to_human. The cast: Pip (owner), Maya (support agent who approves refunds), Dev (the engineer), customers Alex (order #1042, broken pot), Jordan (order #1077), and Sam (order #2001, tries a prompt injection). The three verbs of the course are Analyze (L0–L4), Measure (L5–L7), and Improve (L8–L9). Spec-driven means: write what correct means before building; the prompt, the code, and the evals are all derived from the spec. When the learner wants to go deeper on security than L7 covers (threat modeling, injection, tool misuse, memory poisoning, red-teaming, guards, approval queues, incident response), point them to the platform's course Security and Red-Teaming for Agents, which uses the same Sprout world.
credits: The module and lesson structure follows the public syllabus of "AI Evals for Engineers & PMs" by Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar. All lesson text, examples, quizzes, the glossary, and the Pip's Plant Shop world were written for this course.
